chapters.relation: Foreword by R.K. Stratman, a self-made motorcycle-race T-shirt vendor whose family business grew from iron-on patches at the races to a company of over two hundred employees. He recounts his first ride in a high-school parking lot, his collection of first-and-last engine models including the Buffalo Bike, and names the allure of the ride: freedom on the open road, escape from conformity, and the instant brotherhood of riders whose image has become a pop-culture stereotype. His only contribution to the philosophy of Harley-Davidson is his company's twenty-year slogan: 'If I have to explain, you wouldn't understand.'

Editor Bernard Rollin frames the book with his Yellowstone anecdote: dreading the 'Dreaded Question' about his profession, he confesses to an outlaw biker that he is a philosophy professor and is embraced with 'You have a steady job so you can keep the bike running!' He draws two morals: Harley riders share an instant camaraderie (the trauma surgeon who cursed him for costing him a ride) plus a quiet elitism of being privy to something most people never experience, and bikers treat everything, even careers, as ancillary to time on the motorcycle. The book's essays aim to explain this je ne sais quoi of the Harley way of life.

Priest argues that Pirsig's Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance is far more genuinely Zen than its disclaimer admits: once riding becomes effortless, the dissolution of the subject-object distinction that Dogen calls genjokoan arrives on the open road ('you ARE the driving and the road and the elements'), and the Harley's relaxed posture and low-revving thug-thug-thug rhythm make it a better vehicle for suchness than cars or whinier bikes. Even maintenance done as an end in itself is genjokoan, and because ultimate reality erases every conceptual distinction, care of self, others, and the bike amount to the same thing, the Mahayana ground of compassion; the mountain-and-water Zen saying resolves the paradox that the unconceptualized and the conceptualized are one. Suffering, on the Buddhist diagnosis Priest applies, comes from imposing conceptual grids that see the world wrong, and seeing it aright dissolves it.

Auxier uses the question 'Would Bruce Springsteen ride a Honda?' as an ontological probe: Honda embodies defensible middle-class values while a Harley is not primarily a machine but 'a decision about life and what makes it valuable', a suicide machine Jesus could have ridden into Jerusalem and whose absence would render Easy Rider meaningless even if Fonda rode some other Harley. His own boyhood purchase of a Honda XL 70 over the Harley Z90 becomes a lesson in Heideggerian honesty, since he knew he belonged on a Honda, while buyers who choose for appearances are consumed by das Man, the they-self that lives inauthentically through images and slogans. Using Husserl's method of imaginative variation on the question, he concludes that the Harley as cultural icon represents an existential decision and the life that follows from it.

Over an evening at the Iron Post biker bar, Auxier maps four habitues onto the Hellenistic schools: Cowboy, the Vietnam chopper pilot whose bar is a Garden of modest pleasures, loyalty, and withdrawal from power games, is an Epicurean; the laconic Bear, who doubts that even possessing knowledge would make us better off and suspends judgment, is a Pyrrhonian (unlike the coffee-house Carneadean); Happy Jack, the 'true nature's child' of 'Born to Be Wild' who defies convention and keeps nothing six months, is Diogenes's Cynic; and Gary, the Vietnam-damaged recovering alcoholic, is a damaged Stoic who has not reached apatheia. He concludes that bikers are postmodern pagans whose philosophy is enacted rather than propounded, a Biker Platonism that refuses the Christian-Platonic divorce of body and spirit and lives by honor, freedom, and a pagan fatalism that accepts the consequences of one's choices.

Goldstein applies Hegel's thesis-antithesis-synthesis and Marx's more complex, multidimensional dialectic to the splits within biker culture: bar-room stare-downs as struggles for recognition, wrenchers versus trailers, RUBs versus working-class riders, helmet disputes, and one-percenters versus the rest. He traces the collapse of brotherhood (the clenched fist of solidarity giving way to the selective wave) to the commodification of the motorcycle during the Japanese invasion and to Harley's own yuppie-era Willie G. marketing, arguing via commodity fetishism that bikers misread economic forces between manufacturers as personal differences. His conclusion is that the seeds of unity lie within the divisions, and that Harley-Davidson Motor Co. will not save the culture, since its task is profit, not tradition.

Responding to the Guggenheim's record-breaking 'The Art of the Motorcycle' show, Rollin argues that Dickie's institutional theory explains how motorcycles became art but not why people lined up, and offers three aesthetic lenses: Marinetti's Futurist celebration of machine speed, danger, and rebellion; Dewey's 'an experience', which every ride exemplifies, from his two-week trips with his son to the blown engine rescued by a ranch truck and the canned-spaghetti feast; and the Bauhaus doctrine that form follows function, making customized Harleys industrial sculpture that appreciates in value. He closes with Heidegger: riding's regular face-to-face with 'the possibility of the impossibility of one's being' is a call to authenticity and the final warrant for calling the motorcycle a fountain of aesthetic experience. American Indians revering Harleys as 'iron horses' illustrate the freedom and speed at the core of the bike's aesthetic pull.

Pratt reads the outlaw biker's FTW (Fuck the World) posture as pop-culture nihilism: Nietzsche's 'danger of dangers' and Camus's answer of scorn to an absurd universe ('there is no fate that cannot be surmounted by scorn') are embodied by Brando's Johnny in The Wild One, Sonny Barger's Hells Angels, and the wanton Born to Lose club of The Born Losers, whose smashing matches Pisarev's Russian nihilism. He then shows how Willie G. Davidson's 1977 Low Rider and events like Daytona's Bike Week sanitized and marketed the rebellion, reducing skulls and DILLIGAF patches to ubiquitous fashion worth $340 million a week. Freud supplies the psychology: the superego keeps the rest of us tame, so we voyeuristically buy a tasteful version of outlaw freedom, even though pure nihilism, denying all truth, refutes even itself.

Feldman tests Harley's 'Great American Freedom Machine' slogan against each conception of freedom: metaphysical freedom (universal causation, divine foreknowledge, fate) cannot depend on your vehicle; legal freedom actually shrinks for riders through helmet mandates and extra licensing; and circumstantial freedom is gained equally by any vehicle, a wheelchair being the true freedom machine. Borrowing Socrates' comparison method from the Philebus, he argues the alleged 'feeling of freedom' is really a feeling of happiness or exhilaration combined with the false belief that one is freer than a Camry driver. What really binds him to his 1986 FXRT is fun, the thrill of leaning to the edge, and the sensory and historical pleasures of the air-cooled V-twin line back to the Silent Grey Fellow, which have nothing to do with freedom.

Bourne argues that bikes like the Ducati 916 and Harley V-Rod are genuine works of art: Kantian disinterested attention is both possible and actual (he bought his Ducati Monster on styling alone), and Hume's standard of taste shows that judgments like calling a Honda Gold Wing elegant are answerable to criteria and informed comparison, so taste is not mere subjectivity. Against Wollheim he deploys Currie's account of the artwork as a type of action, so mass-produced instances are no obstacle, exactly as copies of Sartre's Nausea are the same novel; against Danto's aboutness requirement he claims motorcycles are about motorcycles, and should be evaluated like architecture, where function enters the aesthetic judgment. On Bauhaus principles the Ducati 916 expresses its own construction authentically while the V-Rod's styling compromises its ground clearance, which is what makes the Ducati, at least, high art.

Harman argues the real heroes of Easy Rider are the two Harley-Davidsons: the exploding Captain America bike that drowns out its rider's corpse, the cocaine hidden in the gas tank like a prosthetic organ, and the obscured helmets and muffled dialogue reduce Fonda, Hopper, and Nicholson to 'stowaways and parasites' of their machines. He uses this reversal to attack Kant's Copernican Revolution, on which we could know only how Harleys appear to us and never the things in themselves, and to champion the Whitehead-Deleuze-Latour current in which genes, pickup trucks, bridges, and Harleys are autonomous actors no less than humans, against Plato's two-world heir of appearances and unknowable things. Billy and Captain America's 1960s transgression, he concludes, quietly ends in submission to the power, rhythm, and demands of their bikes.

Rollin opposes mandatory helmet laws by contrasting two conceptions of freedom: the Hobbesian absence-of-constraint view ('go to hell in my own way', from Pinocchio's 'no strings on me' to the trapped coyote) and the rational-order view running from Plato (ranked classes, noble lies, censorship, contempt for democracy) through Rousseau's 'forced to be free', which Popper already identified as the enemy of the open society. Since, as the obesity-as-disease example and Robert Paul Wolff's expert-government argument show, we cannot claim certainty about value judgments the way we can about fractures, paternalism fails: if danger justified coercion we would have to ban motorcycles, skiing, parachuting, and bull-riding alike. Helmet laws in effect claim society knows what you ought to want better than you do, and Rollin's answer to his British colleague's 'what will you do if you injure your brain?' is to join the Department of Food Science and Nutrition.

Alford reads the biker image, born at Hollister in 1947 and fixed by The Wild One, through two opposed accounts of presocial man: the badass on his tricked-out Harley is Hobbes's natural man, all vanity, domination, and fear merely redirected to government, praising Chuck Zito's 'most primitive philosophy'; the club run with bonfire, brothers, old ladies, and Steppenwolf re-enacts Rousseau's golden age between the stupidity of brutes and the fatal enlightenment of civil man, before the first enclosed field ('this is mine') bred property, vanity, and misery. The paradox of a biker who is simultaneously threat and salvation dissolves once we see that 'primitive' and 'civilized' are mutually defining: suburbanites and bikers alike live both Hobbesian individualism and Rousseauvian community, each defining themselves against the other.

Ferriss explains biker leather through the two forms of fetishism: Freud's fetish object, by which the black jacket augments masculine potency against castration anxiety (while women riders negotiate pink leather, rhinestones, and the dominatrix option, as Dot Robinson of the Motor Maids did with her lipstick holder), and Marx's commodity fetishism, in which Capital's dancing wooden table becomes the H-D-branded jacket whose exchange value carries Americana and rebellion to dentists, Vogue spreads, Harley Ken dolls, and the Phoenix Art Museum. From Brando's promotional still and Girl on a Motorcycle's 'black bull' to Kenneth Anger's gay Nazi bikers in Scorpio Rising, leather's erotic charge is fashion, a language of gender that changes, and it is now fading as motorcycles themselves become mere accessories in deodorant ads.

Kieffner applies Foucault's deployment of sexuality to show how power centers constructed biker sexual stereotypes: the psychiatric profession behind Time's 1970 'Motorcycle Syndrome', the press that sexualized the Van Buren sisters and filled Easyriders with centerfolds, police 'gauntlets' that pull over bikes but not cars (and ask Raw Thunder's Char Zack if she is a lesbian), and even Harley-Davidson's own 'mystique' video deploying eroticism to sell bikes and HOG memberships. Following Foucault's rule of the tactical polyvalence of discourse, he ends with resistance within the same power structure: riders' rights organizations videotaping police encounters, and the tactical discourses of queer, lesbian, and female riders, from Evelyn Greenway's 1921 'Do it with a motorcycle' onward, who refuse the labels of sexual outlaw and gender traitor.

Jones narrates a day riding a customized Sportster around O'ahu as a lived Daoism that heals the Platonic-Cartesian mind-body split: the ride enacts Zhuangzi's 'rambling without destination' and Cook Ding's effortless wu-wei, rider li (the low hand-greeting among riders) is Confucian ritual propriety, and the island's dry and wet ranges embody yin and yang through whose flow the rider blends. Heraclitus's 'expect the unexpected' and 'the sun is new every day' are vindicated when a container truck stops short and only the disciplined, ego-less low-side, dropping the beloved bike while riding the skid, saves the rider's life, sealing the day's lesson that there is never freedom without discipline. Sartre's hell of other people appears in the cagers' compartmentalized inattention, and the chapter closes with Zhuangzi: 'The way is made by walking it.'

holes.name: Futurism (aesthetics of speed and the machine)
holes.what: Marinetti's 1909 avant-garde movement glorifying speed, machines, danger, and revolt as the beauty of modern life.
holes.why: Chapter 18 quotes the Futurist Manifesto at length and applies it as one of its three aesthetic lenses on the motorcycle's allure.

holes.name: Institutional Theory of Art
holes.what: George Dickie's view that an artifact becomes art when the artworld confers that status on it, as a minister confers marriage.
holes.why: Chapter 18 uses the theory to explain how the Guggenheim exhibit made motorcycles into art while searching other theories for why they deserved it.

holes.name: Nihilism
holes.what: Nietzsche's 'danger of dangers': the collapse of all highest values, so that nothing is true and nothing has inherent value.
holes.why: Chapter 19 is built on nihilism as such, tracing it from Nietzsche and Camus to the outlaw biker's FTW attitude and its commercialization.

holes.name: The Standard of Taste (Hume)
holes.what: Hume's essay arguing aesthetic judgment is not mere subjective preference: informed, unprejudiced critics ground objective standards and genuine disagreement.
holes.why: Chapter 21 leans on it to show that calling a Honda Gold Wing elegant is criticizable and that bike aesthetics is not 'anything goes'.

holes.name: Ontology of Art (type and token)
holes.what: The debate over what a multiple-instance artwork is, contrasting Wollheim's unique physical object with Currie's action-type account.
holes.why: Chapter 21 needs it to explain how a mass-produced Ducati 916 can be one artwork with many instances, like copies of a novel.

holes.name: Object-Oriented Ontology (flat ontology)
holes.what: The view that all objects, human and inanimate, are equally real actors with no privileged human access to the world, rejecting Kant's human-world gap.
holes.why: Chapter 23 uses Easy Rider's Harleys as autonomous heroes to argue exactly this anti-Kantian position, drawing on Whitehead and Latour.

holes.name: Bruno Latour
holes.what: French philosopher of science and actor-network theory who treats humans and nonhumans as equal actors in networks.
holes.why: Chapter 23 names Latour (with Whitehead) as the exemplar of the new object-centered philosophy it endorses through Easy Rider.

holes.name: Fetishism (Freudian)
holes.what: Freud's account of the fetish as an object endowed with power that wards off castration anxiety and manages sexual difference.
holes.why: Chapter 27 explains the black leather jacket as a Freudian fetish object of masculine power before turning to Marx's commodity fetishism.

holes.name: Deployment of Sexuality
holes.what: Foucault's account, in The History of Sexuality, of how institutions incite, classify, and circulate sexual discourse as a technology of power.
holes.why: Chapter 28's entire analysis of biker stereotypes (Motorcycle Syndrome, biker chicks, the police gauntlet) runs on this Foucauldian apparatus.

holes.name: Qi (vital energy)
holes.what: The vital breath or energy flowing through heaven, earth, and the human body in Chinese cosmology, pairing with the five xing processes.
holes.why: Chapter 29 describes the accomplished rider blending with the four qi of heaven and five xing of earth to achieve harmony on the road.
